claim: Active YAP is distributed throughout the murine lung epithelium.
source: We show that active YAP, a key mediator of Hippo signaling, is distributed throughout the murine lung epithelium and loss of epithelial YAP severely disrupts branching.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing nuclear YAP in both SOX2+ and SOX9+ epithelial populations at multiple developmental stages (Figure 1A-P).

claim: Loss of epithelial YAP severely disrupts lung branching morphogenesis.
source: We show that active YAP, a key mediator of Hippo signaling, is distributed throughout the murine lung epithelium and loss of epithelial YAP severely disrupts branching.
evidence: Demonstrated by phenotypic analysis of Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ lungs showing cystic structures and failed branching (Figure 2).

claim: Failure to branch is restricted to regions where YAP activity is removed.
source: Failure to branch is restricted to regions where YAP activity is removed.
evidence: Supported by experiments using different Cre lines (Sox9Cre, spcCre, Nkx2.1Cre) showing localized cyst formation corresponding to regions of YAP deletion (Figure 3).

claim: YAP controls local epithelial cell properties.
source: This suggests that YAP controls local epithelial cell properties.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that localized YAP deletion causes localized branching defects.

claim: Mechanical force production is compromised in Yap mutant lungs.
source: In support of this model, mechanical force production is compromised and cell proliferation is reduced in Yap mutant lungs.
evidence: Demonstrated by reduced pMLC levels, diminished cortical pMLC, and reduced tissue recoil velocity after laser ablation in Yap-deficient lungs (Figure 7).

claim: Cell proliferation is reduced in Yap mutant lungs.
source: In support of this model, mechanical force production is compromised and cell proliferation is reduced in Yap mutant lungs.
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation assays showing reduced epithelial cell proliferation in Yap-deficient lungs (Figure 6).

claim: Defective force generation and insufficient epithelial cell number underlie the branching defects in Yap mutants.
source: We propose that defective force generation and insufficient epithelial cell number underlie the branching defects.
evidence: Based on experimental observations of reduced cell proliferation and compromised mechanical force production in Yap mutants.

claim: YAP controls pMLC levels through a feedback mechanism.
source: Through genomic analysis, we also uncovered a feedback control of pMLC levels, which is critical for mechanical force production, likely through the direct induction of multiple regulators by YAP.
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq and ChIP-Seq data identifying YAP targets (Arhgef17, Bcam, S1pr2, Nuak2) that regulate pMLC levels (Figure 5).

claim: Nuclear YAP is found in both SOX2+ (proximal) and SOX9+ (distal) epithelial populations at 11.5, 12.5 and 14.5 dpc.
source: Nuclear YAP could be found in both SOX2+ (proximal) and SOX9+ (distal) epithelial populations in wild-type lungs at 11.5, 12.5 and 14.5 dpc (Figure 1A–P; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that YAP is active throughout the lung epithelium.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining showing nuclear YAP in both epithelial populations.

claim: YAP staining was barely detectable in the epithelium but present at wild-type levels in the mesenchyme of Yap-deficient lungs.
source: YAP staining was barely detectable in the epithelium but was present at wild-type levels in the mesenchyme of Yap-deficient (Yapf/f; ShhCre/+) lungs (see below) (Figure 1Q,R; Figure 1—figure supplement 1M), indicating the specificity of YAP antibodies.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining of Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ lungs showing loss of epithelial YAP but retention in mesenchyme.

claim: A high percentage of SOX2+ cells and SOX9+ cells displayed nuclear YAP staining in wild-type lungs.
source: A high percentage of SOX2+ cells and SOX9+ cells displayed nuclear YAP staining in wild-type lungs (Figure 1S).
evidence: Quantified data showing nuclear YAP in both proximal and distal epithelial cells.

claim: CTGF, an established YAP target, is expressed in both the proximal and distal airways.
source: Consistent with the distribution of active YAP along the entire lung epithelium, expression of connective tissue growth factor (CTGF), an established YAP target, was detected in both the proximal and distal airways (Figure 1T–V).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining showing CTGF expression in both airway regions.

claim: There is no sharp transition of YAP from the cytoplasm to the nucleus at the junction between the SOX2+ and SOX9+ populations.
source: We did not observe a sharp transition of YAP from the cytoplasm to the nucleus at the junction between the SOX2+ and SOX9+ populations, a region dubbed the transition zone (TZ) (Figure 1W), as previously reported (Mahoney et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on immunofluorescence observations showing nuclear YAP throughout the epithelium without a sharp transition.

claim: Phosphorylated YAP (pYAP) is present in both SOX2+ and SOX9+ epithelial cells.
source: We found that phosphorylated YAP (pYAP) was present in both SOX2+ and SOX9+ epithelial cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining for pYAP in lung sections.

claim: pYAP levels are generally higher in the proximal than distal epithelium.
source: pYAP levels were, in general, higher in the proximal than distal epithelium, but pYAP levels varied significantly from cell to cell in both the proximal and distal airways (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Observed through immunostaining showing differential pYAP levels.

claim: Low levels of pYAP are associated with the presence of nuclear YAP in many cells.
source: Nevertheless, in many cells, low levels of pYAP were associated with the presence of nuclear YAP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Observed through co-immunostaining of pYAP and YAP.

claim: Lung epithelial cells without nuclear YAP usually stain positive for cytoplasmic YAP.
source: Lung epithelial cells that do not have nuclear YAP usually stain positive for cytoplasmic YAP.
evidence: Observed through YAP immunostaining showing cytoplasmic localization in some cells.

claim: YAP exhibits dynamic shuttling and distribution along the entire airway epithelium.
source: This is consistent with a model in which pYAP is sequestered and degraded in the cytoplasm, but it also indicates a dynamic shuttling and distribution of YAP along the entire airway epithelium (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: Inferred from the observation of both nuclear and cytoplasmic YAP in different cells and the presence of pYAP.

claim: The lungs of Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ embryos consisted of a few large, thin-layered cysts.
source: The lungs of Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ embryos (called Yap mutants hereafter) (Figure 2A–H) consisted of a few large, thin-layered cysts, which replaced normal lung tissue and eliminated lung function (Figure 2C,G,D,H).
evidence: Demonstrated by histological and gross morphological analysis of mutant lungs.

claim: Cystic lung structures in Yap mutants replaced normal lung tissue and eliminated lung function.
source: The lungs of Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ embryos (called Yap mutants hereafter) (Figure 2A–H) consisted of a few large, thin-layered cysts, which replaced normal lung tissue and eliminated lung function (Figure 2C,G,D,H).
evidence: Inferred from the severe cystic phenotype and neonatal lethality.

claim: No apparent difference in the morphology of lung buds was observed between wild-type and Yap mutants at 10.5 dpc.
source: (A,E) Hematoxylin and eosin-stained sections of wild-type and Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ embryos at 10.5 dpc. No apparent difference in the morphology of lung buds was observed between wild-type and Yap mutants.
evidence: Demonstrated by histological comparison at 10.5 dpc.

claim: Five buds were produced in both control and Yap-deficient lungs at 11.5 dpc.
source: (B,C,F,G) Ventral view of dissected lungs from wild-type and Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ mice at 11.5 and 18.5 dpc. Five buds were produced in both control and Yap-deficient lungs at 11.5 dpc; defective lung branching along the entire lung epithelium could already be detected at this stage in Yap mutants.
evidence: Demonstrated by gross morphological analysis of dissected lungs.

claim: Defective lung branching along the entire lung epithelium could be detected at 11.5 dpc in Yap mutants.
source: (B,C,F,G) Ventral view of dissected lungs from wild-type and Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ mice at 11.5 and 18.5 dpc. Five buds were produced in both control and Yap-deficient lungs at 11.5 dpc; defective lung branching along the entire lung epithelium could already be detected at this stage in Yap mutants.
evidence: Demonstrated by morphological analysis showing abnormal branching patterns.

claim: Failure to execute a stereotyped program of branching in the absence of Yap resulted in lungs consisting only of multiple cysts at 18.5 dpc.
source: As lung development proceeded, failure to execute a stereotyped program of branching in the absence of Yap resulted in lungs consisting only of multiple cysts at 18.5 dpc.
evidence: Demonstrated by gross morphological and histological analysis at 18.5 dpc.

claim: Cell types in the proximal airway of Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ mice failed to be specified.
source: (D,H) Immunostaining of lung sections collected from wild-type and Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ mice at 18.5 dpc. Cell types in the proximal airway of Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ mice failed to be specified. For instance, expression of markers for Clara [club] cells (CC10+), ciliated cells (acetylated-tubulin [Ac-tub]+) and pulmonary neuroendocrine cells (CGRP+) were barely detectable (not shown).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining showing loss of cell-type specific markers.

claim: Expression of markers for Clara cells (CC10+), ciliated cells (acetylated-tubulin+) and pulmonary neuroendocrine cells (CGRP+) were barely detectable in Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ lungs.
source: For instance, expression of markers for Clara [club] cells (CC10+), ciliated cells (acetylated-tubulin [Ac-tub]+) and pulmonary neuroendocrine cells (CGRP+) were barely detectable (not shown).
evidence: Stated as observation from immunostaining experiments.

claim: Reduction in the expression of distal lung cell markers, such as SPC (type II cells) and T1α (type I cells), in the cysts of Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ lungs was noted.
source: Reduction in the expression of distal lung cell markers, such as SPC (type II cells) and T1α (type I cells), in the cysts of Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ lungs was also noted.
evidence: Observed through immunostaining of distal cell markers.

claim: Defective lung development was already apparent at 11.5 dpc in Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ lungs prior to stereotyped branching and cell differentiation.
source: Defective lung development was already apparent at 11.5 dpc in Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ lungs (Figure 2A,B,E,F) prior to stereotyped branching and cell differentiation.
evidence: Demonstrated by morphological analysis at early developmental stages.

claim: The mutant lung buds failed to produce five fully separated buds.
source: The mutant lung buds failed to produce five fully separated buds.
evidence: Observed through gross morphological analysis of dissected lungs.

claim: The buds that will produce the future cranial and middle lobes remained largely connected in Yap mutants.
source: In particular, the buds that will produce the future cranial and middle lobes remained largely connected (Figure 2B,N; Figure 3F).
evidence: Demonstrated by morphological analysis showing incomplete lobe separation.

claim: The limited branching in Yap mutants came to a halt around 13.5 dpc.
source: While stereotyped branching was actively underway in the wild-type lungs, the limited branching in Yap mutants came to a halt around 13.5 dpc (Figure 2I–R).
evidence: Observed through time-course morphological analysis.

claim: In the absence of Yap, unbranched lung buds enlarged during development and turned into a multi-cyst structure.
source: In the absence of Yap, unbranched lung buds enlarged during development and turned into a multi-cyst structure.
evidence: Demonstrated by morphological analysis at multiple developmental stages.

claim: Cystic lung defects in Yap mutants affect all lobes and can be observed at very early stages of lung development, preceding expression of definitive epithelial markers.
source: It is important to point out that cystic lung defects in Yap mutants that affect all lobes can be observed at very early stages of lung development, preceding expression of definitive epithelial markers.
evidence: Observed through developmental time-course analysis.

claim: The early onset of cystic defects is consistent with a model in which YAP regulates the behavior of all epithelial cells.
source: This would be consistent with a model in which YAP regulates the behavior of all epithelial cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that defects occur before cell differentiation.

claim: Lung cysts in Yapf/f; Sox9Cre/+ and Yapf/f; spcCre/+ mice were largely confined to the distal airway.
source: (A–D) Ventral view of dissected lungs from wild-type, Yapf/f; Sox9Cre/+, Yapf/f; spcCre/+ and Yapf/f; Nkx2.1Cre/+ mice at 18.5 dpc. Lung cysts in Yapf/f; Sox9Cre/+ and Yapf/f; spcCre/+ mice were largely confined to the distal airway (arrows in B,C), while lung cysts were found in the upper lobes (arrow in D) of Yapf/f; Nkx2.1Cre/+ mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by morphological analysis of lungs with different Cre drivers.

claim: Lung cysts were found in the upper lobes of Yapf/f; Nkx2.1Cre/+ mice.
source: Lung cysts in Yapf/f; Sox9Cre/+ and Yapf/f; spcCre/+ mice were largely confined to the distal airway (arrows in B,C), while lung cysts were found in the upper lobes (arrow in D) of Yapf/f; Nkx2.1Cre/+ mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by morphological analysis showing localized cyst formation.

claim: The location of lung cyst formation is correlated with the sites of strong Cre activity and Yap removal.
source: The location of lung cyst formation is correlated with the sites of strong Cre activity and Yap removal. This suggests that loss of Yap at a given region leads to localized lung cysts.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing Cre expression patterns with cyst locations across different Cre lines.

claim: Loss of Yap at a given region leads to localized lung cysts.
source: This suggests that loss of Yap at a given region leads to localized lung cysts.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between Cre activity patterns and cyst locations.

claim: Branching defects and cyst formation in Yapf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs did not appear until 13.5 dpc.
source: (E–N) Whole-mount immunostaining of dissected lungs from wild-type, Yapf/f; ShhCre/+, Yapf/f; Sox9Cre/+, Yapf/f; spcCre/+ and Yapf/f; Nkx2.1Cre/+ mice at the stages indicated. Lung epithelium was visualized by E-cadherin (E-cad). While defective branching was apparent in Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ lungs at 11.5 dpc, branching defects and cyst formation in Yapf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs did not appear until 13.5 dpc.
evidence: Demonstrated by time-course morphological analysis.

claim: Cyst formation in Yapf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs was confined to the distal airways.
source: Cyst formation in Yapf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs was confined to the distal airways (arrow in K).
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunostaining showing localized cysts.

claim: Cyst formation in Yapf/f; spcCre/+ lungs was detected primarily in the distal airways.
source: Similarly, cyst formation in Yapf/f; spcCre/+ lungs was detected primarily in the distal airways (arrows in M).
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunostaining.

claim: Cyst formation was found in the upper lobes of Yapf/f; Nkx2.1Cre/+ lungs.
source: By contrast, cyst formation was found in the upper lobes (arrow in N) of Yapf/f; Nkx2.1Cre/+ lungs.
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunostaining.

claim: YAP was lost primarily in distal airways in Yapf/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice.
source: (E–L) YAP was lost primarily in distal airways in Yapf/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice, while sporadic loss of YAP can be found in the proximal airway.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining for YAP in Sox9Cre mutant lungs.

claim: Removal of YAP in distal airways of Yapf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs at 12.5 dpc is associated with loss of CTGF, a direct YAP target.
source: (M–T) Removal of YAP in distal airways (dotted lines in T) of Yapf/f; Sox9Cre/+ lungs at 12.5 dpc is associated with loss of CTGF, a direct YAP target.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunostaining for YAP and CTGF.

claim: Lung cyst formation in distal airways of Yapf/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice is due to loss of YAP in the distal airway.
source: Together, these results suggest that lung cyst formation in distal airways of Yapf/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice is due to loss of YAP in the distal airway.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between YAP loss and cyst location.

claim: High levels of spcCre expression were largely confined to the distal airway.
source: (A–D) Immunostaining of lung sections collected from Yapf/f; spcCre/+ mice at 13.5 days post coitus (dpc). SOX2 expression marks the proximal airway, while the distal airway is distinguished by SOX9 expression (not shown). High levels of spcCre expression were largely confined to the distal airway, where spcCre expression in a given epithelial cell was correlated with loss of YAP immunoreactivity (e.g. arrowheads in D).
evidence: Demonstrated by Cre immunostaining in spcCre mice.

claim: spcCre expression in a given epithelial cell was correlated with loss of YAP immunoreactivity.
source: High levels of spcCre expression were largely confined to the distal airway, where spcCre expression in a given epithelial cell was correlated with loss of YAP immunoreactivity (e.g. arrowheads in D).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunostaining for Cre and YAP.

claim: YAP was lost mainly in distal airways in Yapf/f; spcCre/+ mice.
source: (E–H) Immunostaining of lung sections collected from Yapf/f; spcCre/+ mice at 14.5 dpc. Only distal airways are shown. YAP was lost mainly in distal airways in Yapf/f; spcCre/+ mice while sporadic loss of YAP was found in the proximal airway.
evidence: Demonstrated by YAP immunostaining in spcCre mutant lungs.

claim: Lung cyst formation in distal airways of Yapf/f; spcCre/+ mice is due to loss of YAP in the distal airway.
source: Together, these results suggest that lung cyst formation in distal airways of Yapf/f; spcCre/+ mice is due to loss of YAP in the distal airway.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between YAP loss and cyst location.

claim: YAP was lost mainly in the upper lobe in Yapf/f; Nkx2.1Cre/+ lung.
source: (A–D) Immunostaining of lung sections collected from Yapf/f; Nkx2.1Cre/+ mice at 14.5 days post coitus (dpc). SOX2 expression marks the proximal airway, while the distal airway is distinguished by SOX9 expression (not shown). YAP was lost mainly in the upper lobe in Yapf/f; Nkx2.1Cre/+ lung.
evidence: Demonstrated by YAP immunostaining in Nkx2.1Cre mutant lungs.

claim: Lung cyst formation was primarily observed in the distal airway of Yapf/f; Nkx2.1Cre/+ lungs.
source: Lung cyst formation was primarily observed in the distal airway.
evidence: Observed through morphological analysis.

claim: Sox2 expression was present in sporadic Yap-deficient cells in the transition zone induced by Sox9Cre, spcCre or Nkx2.1Cre.
source: Sox2 expression was present in sporadic Yap-deficient cells in the transition zone induced by Sox9Cre, spcCre or Nkx2.1Cre. This suggests that Sox2 expression is not controlled by YAP.
evidence: Observed through immunostaining for Sox2 in Yap-deficient cells.

claim: Sox2 expression is not controlled by YAP.
source: This suggests that Sox2 expression is not controlled by YAP.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Sox2 is expressed in Yap-deficient cells.

claim: Two copies of Nkx2.1Cre enhanced the cystic lung phenotype.
source: (A–D) Hematoxylin and eosin-stained sections of lungs from wild-type, Yapf/f; Nkx2.1Cre/+ (one copy of Nkx2.1Cre), Yapf/f; Nkx2.1Cre/Cre (two copies of Nkx2.1Cre) and Yapf/f; spcCre/+ (one copy of spcCre) mice at 18.5 dpc. Removal of Yap was more efficient when two copies of Nkx2.1Cre or spcCre were present and lungs phenotypes were more severe.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing phenotypes with different Cre copy numbers.

claim: Removal of Yap was more efficient when two copies of Nkx2.1Cre or spcCre were present and lung phenotypes were more severe.
source: Removal of Yap was more efficient when two copies of Nkx2.1Cre or spcCre were present and lungs phenotypes were more severe.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing phenotypes with different Cre copy numbers.

claim: Cell types in the proximal airway or regions where no cysts were present appeared to be properly specified in Yapf/f; Nkx2.1Cre/Cre, Yapf/f; spcCre/+, and Yapf/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice.
source: (E–H) Immunostaining of lung sections collected from Yapf/f; Nkx2.1Cre/+, Yapf/f; Nkx2.1Cre/Cre, Yapf/f; spcCre/+ and Yapf/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice at 18.5 dpc. While more lung cysts were detected in Yapf/f; Nkx2.1Cre/Cre mice than Yapf/f; Nkx2.1Cre/+ mice, cell types in the proximal airway or regions where no cysts were present appeared to be properly specified as indicated by their expression of CC10 (Clara cell marker) and acetylated-tubulin [Ac-tub] (ciliated cell marker). Similarly, cell types in the proximal airway were specified in Yapf/f; spcCre/+ and Yapf/f; Sox9Cre/+ mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining for cell-type markers.

claim: Lung cyst formation is correlated with Cre activity and is independent of proximal airway specification.
source: This suggests that lung cyst formation is correlated with Cre activity and is independent of proximal airway specification.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that proximal cell types are specified despite cyst formation in distal regions.

claim: Expression of SOX2 and markers of proximal cell types appeared to be well maintained in Yapf/f; Sox9Cre/+, Yapf/f; spcCre/+, and Yapf/f; Nkx2.1Cre/+ lungs.
source: Indeed, we discovered that expression of SOX2 and markers of proximal cell types appeared to be well maintained in Yapf/f; Sox9Cre/+ and Yapf/f; spcCre/+ (and even in Yapf/f; Nkx2.1Cre/+) lungs (Figure 4A–H; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining for SOX2 and proximal cell markers.

claim: Production of lung cell types in the more proximal airways, such as Clara cells (CC10+), ciliated cells (Ac-tubulin+) and pulmonary neuroendocrine cells (CGRP+), in Yapf/f; Sox9Cre/+ and Yapf/f; spcCre/+ lungs was indistinguishable from that in control lungs.
source: For instance, production of lung cell types in the more proximal airways, such as Clara [club] cells (CC10 [Scgb1a1]+), ciliated cells (Ac-tubulin+) and pulmonary neuroendocrine cells (CGRP+), in Yapf/f; Sox9Cre/+ and Yapf/f; spcCre/+ lungs was indistinguishable from that in control lungs.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining for cell-type markers.

claim: The generation of distal cell types, including alveolar type II cells (SPC+, SPB+, SPD+) and type I cells (T1α+, Aqp5+), was severely affected in Yapf/f; Sox9Cre/+ and Yapf/f; spcCre/+ lungs.
source: As expected from distal cyst formation, the generation of distal cell types, including alveolar type II cells (SPC+, SPB+, SPD+) and type I cells (T1α+, Aqp5+), was severely affected in Yapf/f; Sox9Cre/+ and Yapf/f; spcCre/+ lungs.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining for distal cell markers.

claim: Disruption of branching is associated with defective cell-type specification locally.
source: This suggests that disruption of branching is associated with defective cell-type specification locally.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that distal cell types are affected in regions with cysts.

claim: Cyst formation can be independent of proximal cell-type specification.
source: In addition, cyst formation can be independent of proximal cell-type specification.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that proximal cell types are specified despite cyst formation.

claim: Lung branches or cysts with proper apical aPKC, subapical ZO1/ZO2 and basolateral Laminin could be observed in Yap mutants at 11.5, 12.5 and 14.5 dpc.
source: We showed that lung branches or cysts with proper apical aPKC, subapical ZO1/ZO2 and basolateral Laminin could be observed in Yap mutants at 11.5, 12.5 and 14.5 dpc (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining for polarity markers.

claim: Lung epithelial cell polarity is not disrupted in the absence of YAP.
source: This suggests that lung epithelial cell polarity is not disrupted in the absence of YAP.
evidence: Inferred from the proper localization of polarity markers in Yap mutants.

claim: No apparent alterations in markers for tight junctions (e.g. ZO1, ZO2) and adherens junctions (e.g. E-cadherin, β-catenin and α-catenin) were found between control and Yap mutant lungs.
source: We also examined possible changes in cell junctions in Yap-deficient lungs. No apparent alterations in markers for tight junctions (e.g. ZO1, ZO2) and adherens junctions (e.g. E-cadherin, β-catenin and α-catenin) were found between control and Yap mutant lungs (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining for junction markers.

claim: Loss of YAP does not perturb cell junctions at the light microscopy level.
source: Thus, loss of YAP does not perturb cell junctions at the light microscopy level.
evidence: Inferred from the normal distribution of junction markers in Yap mutants.

claim: Genes that control the cell cycle and cellular contractility topped the cluster of differentially expressed genes in RNA-Seq analysis of control and Yap-deficient lungs.
source: To understand how disruption of local epithelial properties leads to defective lung branching and cyst formation, we performed RNA-Seq analysis on control and Yap-deficient lungs at 12.5 and 14.5 dpc, and similar results were obtained at both stages. Genes that control the cell cycle and cellular contractility topped the cluster of differentially expressed genes (Figure 5A,C).
evidence: Demonstrated by pathway analysis of RNA-Seq data.

claim: Known YAP targets (such as Ctgf, Ajuba and Amotl2) were identified in ChIP-Seq analysis.
source: We showed that known YAP targets (such as Ctgf, Ajuba and Amotl2) were identified in this approach (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by ChIP-Seq showing YAP enrichment at known target genes.

claim: Many new YAP targets were uncovered by ChIP-Seq analysis.
source: Many new YAP targets were also uncovered.
evidence: Stated as result from ChIP-Seq analysis.

claim: Many YAP targets identified by RNA-Seq and ChIP-Seq are involved in regulating the cell cycle (e.g. Ccne1) and cellular contractility (such as Arhgef17, Bcam, S1pr2 and Nuak2).
source: Analysis of both RNA-Seq and ChIP-Seq data allowed us to identify a list of YAP targets that not only have a reduced expression in Yap mutant lungs but also have a TEAD-binding site within the ChIP-Seq peak in their promoter/enhancer. Many of these YAP targets are involved in regulating the cell cycle (e.g. Ccne1) and cellular contractility (such as Arhgef17, Bcam, S1pr2 and Nuak2) (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: Demonstrated by integrated analysis of RNA-Seq and ChIP-Seq data.

claim: Hippo signaling reciprocally controls the actomyosin cytoskeleton and mechanical force production.
source: While cell adhesion/tight junctions and the cytoskeleton have been shown to influence Hippo signaling (Matsui and Lai, 2013; Dupont et al., 2011), our new findings suggest that Hippo signaling reciprocally controls the actomyosin cytoskeleton and mechanical force production.
evidence: Inferred from the identification of YAP targets that regulate cellular contractility.

claim: The rate of cell proliferation in Yap-deficient lung epithelium was reduced.
source: We noticed that the rate of cell proliferation in Yap-deficient lung epithelium was reduced, while mesenchymal cell proliferation was unaffected in the absence of YAP (Figure 6A–C and data not shown).
evidence: Demonstrated by EdU incorporation assays.

claim: Mesenchymal cell proliferation was unaffected in the absence of YAP.
source: We noticed that the rate of cell proliferation in Yap-deficient lung epithelium was reduced, while mesenchymal cell proliferation was unaffected in the absence of YAP (Figure 6A–C and data not shown).
evidence: Demonstrated by EdU incorporation assays showing no change in mesenchymal proliferation.

claim: Decreased cell proliferation in Yap mutant lungs would lower the number of epithelial cells and contribute to the failure of lung branching.
source: Decreased cell proliferation in Yap mutant lungs would lower the number of epithelial cells and contribute to the failure of lung branching in Yap mutants.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of reduced proliferation in Yap mutants.

claim: The rate of cell death by TUNEL assay was unaltered in the absence of Yap.
source: In contrast, the rate of cell death by TUNEL assay was unaltered in the absence of Yap (data not shown).
evidence: Stated as observation from TUNEL assays.

claim: Cell death is neither a key factor in mediating YAP activity in the lung nor a contributor to cyst formation in the absence of YAP.
source: Thus, cell death is neither a key factor in mediating YAP activity in the lung nor a contributor to cyst formation in the absence of YAP.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that cell death is unaltered in Yap mutants.

claim: pMLC protein levels were significantly diminished in Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ lungs.
source: We found that pMLC protein levels were significantly diminished in Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ lungs (Figure 7A; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis.

claim: Cortical pMLC, which is associated with mechanical force production during morphogenesis, is disrupted in the absence of Yap.
source: This led to our speculation that cortical pMLC, which is associated with mechanical force production during morphogenesis is disrupted in the absence of Yap.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of reduced pMLC levels.

claim: In wild-type lungs, cortical pMLC was distributed in both epithelial and mesenchymal cells at 11.5 dpc.
source: In wild-type lungs, cortical pMLC was distributed in both epithelial and mesenchymal cells at 11.5 dpc (Figure 7D–F).
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunofluorescence and two-photon microscopy.

claim: Cortical pMLC was drastically reduced in the epithelium but retained normal levels in the mesenchyme of Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ lungs at 11.5 dpc.
source: By contrast, cortical pMLC was drastically reduced in the epithelium but retained normal levels in the mesenchyme of Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ lungs at 11.5 dpc (Figure 7G–I).
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunofluorescence and two-photon microscopy.

claim: Laser ablation of lung epithelial cells triggered recoiling of non-injured neighboring cells in control but not in Yap-deficient lungs.
source: (J–M) Laser ablation of control and Yapf/f; ShhCre/+; ROSA26mTmG/+ lungs. Lung epithelial cells were labeled by GFP from the ROSA26mTmG/+ allele induced by ShhCre. Laser ablation of lung epithelial cells by two-photon microscopy (indicated by bars in J,L) triggered recoiling of non-injured neighboring cells in control but not in Yap-deficient lungs (see Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by laser ablation experiments and time-lapse imaging.

claim: The velocity of recoil was reduced in Yap-deficient lungs compared to that of control lungs.
source: (R) The velocity of epithelial recoil was measured in control and Yap-deficient lungs after laser ablation. A reduction in velocity was found in the absence of YAP (n ≥ 6 for each group).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of recoil velocity after laser ablation.

claim: The initial velocity of the recoil in the first few seconds post-ablation is proportional to the magnitude of the resting tension.
source: The initial velocity of the recoil in the first few seconds post-ablation is shown to be proportional to the magnitude of the resting tension (Hutson et al., 2003).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: Reduction in cortical pMLC at very early stages of lung development (prior to cell differentiation) would compromise mechanical force production and lead to defective branching.
source: We propose that reduction in cortical pMLC at very early stages of lung development (prior to cell differentiation) would compromise mechanical force production and lead to defective branching.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of reduced cortical pMLC at early stages in Yap mutants.

claim: Altered epithelial cell properties underlie the lung abnormalities in Yap mutants.
source: This further suggests that altered epithelial cell properties underlie the lung abnormalities in Yap mutants.
evidence: Inferred from the observations of reduced proliferation and mechanical force production.

claim: The mRNA levels of Arhgef17 were reduced in Yap-deficient lungs by RNA-Seq and qPCR analysis.
source: We found that the mRNA levels of Arhgef17 (encoding a RhoGEF) were reduced in Yap-deficient lungs by RNA-Seq and qPCR analysis (Figure 5D).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-Seq and qPCR.

claim: ChIP-Seq analysis of YAP identified a peak in the Arhgef17 promoter, which contains a conserved TEAD-binding site.
source: Notably, ChIP-Seq analysis of YAP identified a peak in the Arhgef17 promoter, which contains a conserved TEAD-binding site.
evidence: Demonstrated by ChIP-Seq analysis.

claim: Both YAP and TEAD reside in the Arhgef17 promoter in embryonic lungs at 14.5 dpc.
source: We showed that both YAP and TEAD reside in the Arhgef17 promoter in embryonic lungs at 14.5 dpc by ChIP-qPCR analysis (Figure 5E), indicating that Arhgef17 is a direct YAP target.
evidence: Demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR.

claim: Arhgef17 is a direct YAP target.
source: We showed that both YAP and TEAD reside in the Arhgef17 promoter in embryonic lungs at 14.5 dpc by ChIP-qPCR analysis (Figure 5E), indicating that Arhgef17 is a direct YAP target.
evidence: Inferred from ChIP-Seq and ChIP-qPCR data showing YAP/TEAD binding to Arhgef17 promoter.

claim: ARHGEF17 is an effector of YAP in controlling a Rho–ROCK-pMLC cascade and mechanical force production.
source: This suggests that ARHGEF17 is an effector of YAP in controlling a Rho–ROCK-pMLC cascade and mechanical force production.
evidence: Inferred from the identification of Arhgef17 as a YAP target and its known role in RhoA activation.

claim: YAP controls pMLC levels and mechanical force production through multiple pathways, including a YAP–RhoGEF–RhoA–ROCK pathway.
source: We surmise that YAP controls pMLC levels and mechanical force production through multiple pathways, including a YAP–RhoGEF–RhoA–ROCK pathway (Figure 7S).
evidence: Inferred from the identification of multiple YAP targets that regulate pMLC.

claim: RNA-Seq and ChIP-Seq analyses uncovered several new YAP targets that regulate pMLC levels via different mechanisms, including Bcam, S1pr2 and Nuak2.
source: Indeed, our RNA-Seq and ChIP-Seq analyses uncovered several new YAP targets that regulate pMLC levels via different mechanisms. They include the Laminin alpha 5 receptor (Bcam), Sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor 2 (S1pr2) and NUAK family, SNF1-like kinase, 2 (Nuak2).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-Seq and ChIP-Seq analysis.

claim: Expression of Bcam, S1pr2 and Nuak2 was downregulated in the absence of YAP.
source: Expression of these genes was downregulated in the absence of YAP.
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-Seq analysis.

claim: Conserved TEAD-binding sites were found in the promoters of Bcam, S1pr2 and Nuak2.
source: Furthermore, conserved TEAD-binding sites were found in the promoters of Bcam, S1pr2 and Nuak2 (Figure 5C), where the YAP and TEAD proteins reside as revealed by ChIP-Seq and ChIP-qPCR analysis (Figure 5E).
evidence: Demonstrated by ChIP-Seq and ChIP-qPCR analysis.

claim: BCAM and S1PR2 can activate RhoA to promote pMLC production.
source: BCAM and S1PR2 can activate RhoA (Collec et al., 2011; Randriamboavonjy et al., 2009) to promote pMLC production.
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: NUAK2 kinase can enhance pMLC generation by inhibiting MLC phosphatase independently of RhoA.
source: The NUAK2 kinase can also enhance pMLC generation by inhibiting MLC phosphatase independently of RhoA (Zagórska et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: YAP could control pMLC levels and mechanical force production through an elaborate signaling network.
source: Our results suggest that YAP could control pMLC levels and mechanical force production through an elaborate signaling network (Figure 7S).
evidence: Inferred from the identification of multiple YAP targets that regulate pMLC through different mechanisms.

claim: Reduced cell number and disrupted mechanical force generation contribute to defective branching in Yap mutant lungs.
source: Our work provides new insight into the molecular mechanisms by which YAP controls lung development. We propose that reduced cell number and disrupted mechanical force generation contribute to defective branching in Yap mutant lungs.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations of reduced proliferation and mechanical force in Yap mutants.

claim: Mechanical force production via regulation of pMLC levels could play a central role in lung branching during development.
source: Previous studies reported abnormal lung branching through pharmacological manipulation of Rho, ROCK or the actomyosin cytoskeleton in ex vivo lung culture (Moore et al., 2005). This is consistent with our model in which mechanical force production via regulation of pMLC levels could play a central role in lung branching during development.
evidence: Inferred from current findings and cited literature on Rho/ROCK manipulation.

claim: Control of tissue tension by YAP has been described in medaka embryos.
source: Control of tissue tension by YAP has been described in medaka embryos (Porazinski et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: ARHGAP18 was reported to be an effector of YAP in medaka embryos.
source: Interestingly, ARHGAP18 was reported to be an effector of YAP in that study.
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: The Hippo pathway can regulate F-actin accumulation in Drosophila.
source: Moreover, the Hippo pathway can regulate F-actin accumulation in Drosophila (Gaspar and Tapon, 2014) and YAP regulates genes that control cell cycle progression, F-actin polymerization and actin cytoskeleton remodeling in the mammalian heart (Morikawa et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: YAP regulates genes that control cell cycle progression, F-actin polymerization and actin cytoskeleton remodeling in the mammalian heart.
source: Moreover, the Hippo pathway can regulate F-actin accumulation in Drosophila (Gaspar and Tapon, 2014) and YAP regulates genes that control cell cycle progression, F-actin polymerization and actin cytoskeleton remodeling in the mammalian heart (Morikawa et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: Genes regulated by YAP in the heart were proposed to function in cell migration.
source: These genes were proposed to function in cell migration in the heart.
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: The actin cytoskeleton itself does not generate mechanical force.
source: The actin cytoskeleton itself does not generate mechanical force.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge of cytoskeletal mechanics.

claim: Mechanical force production is mediated by contraction of myosin in the actomyosin cytoskeleton.
source: Mechanical force production is mediated by contraction of myosin in the actomyosin cytoskeleton, a network composed of myosin associated with F-actin bundles.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge of actomyosin contractility.

claim: Classical transplantation studies have revealed the inductive ability of the mesenchyme in epithelial branching.
source: Indeed, classical transplantation studies have revealed the inductive ability of the mesenchyme in epithelial branching.
evidence: Cited from established knowledge in the field.

claim: Recent studies suggest the involvement of mesenchymal smooth muscle in epithelial branching.
source: Interestingly, recent studies suggest the involvement of mesenchymal smooth muscle in epithelial branching (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: YAP is dynamically shuttling in and out of the nucleus along the entire lung epithelium.
source: We reported mosaic patterns of nuclear YAP distribution in lung epithelium. pYAP levels also vary significantly from cell to cell in both the proximal and distal airways, and a lower pYAP level is usually associated with nuclear localization of YAP. This suggests that YAP is dynamically shuttling in and out of the nucleus along the entire lung epithelium.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of variable YAP and pYAP levels in different cells.

claim: On average, 30–50% proximal and 10–28% distal epithelial cells contain cytoplasmic YAP.
source: On the average, 30–50% proximal and 10–28% distal epithelial cells contain cytoplasmic YAP, which is presumed to be inactive.
evidence: Inferred from quantification data showing nuclear YAP percentages.

claim: Epithelial cells that undergo active branching need to maintain active YAP signaling.
source: It is likely epithelial cells that undergo active branching need to maintain active YAP signaling.
evidence: Speculated based on the correlation between YAP activity and branching.

claim: Epithelial cells not actively branching may have inactive YAP through YAP phosphorylation.
source: By contrast, epithelial cells not actively branching may have inactive YAP through YAP phosphorylation.
evidence: Speculated based on the observation of variable YAP activity.

claim: Deletion of cytoplasmic YAP by Cre is not expected to exert non-cell autonomous effects on neighboring cells that contain nuclear YAP.
source: If cytoplasmic YAP is inactive as postulated, we anticipate that deletion of YAP in these cells should not have significant functional consequences. Namely, deletion of cytoplasmic YAP by Cre is not expected to exert non-cell autonomous effects on neighboring cells that contain nuclear YAP.
evidence: Speculated based on the assumption that cytoplasmic YAP is inactive.

claim: pMLC is only produced and/or maintained at active sites of branching.
source: As an extension of these ideas, we propose that pMLC is only produced and/or maintained at active sites of branching.
evidence: Speculated based on the role of pMLC in mechanical force production.

claim: pMLC exhibits dynamical patterns in the epithelial membrane during branching morphogenesis.
source: Consistent with this idea, pMLC was shown to exhibit dynamical patterns in the epithelial membrane during branching morphogenesis (Schnatwinkel and Niswander, 2013).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: New bud formation requires increased mechanical tension at the apical surface for its expansion and protrusion to produce new buds, while less tension is present in the interbud region.
source: One possibility is that new bud formation requires increased mechanical tension at the apical surface for its expansion and protrusion to produce new buds, while less tension is present in the interbud region.
evidence: Speculated based on the role of mechanical force in branching.

claim: The trachea and main stem bronchi appear to be spared in Yap mutants induced by ShhCre.
source: Loss of YAP induced by ShhCre resulted in global cystic formation. It is interesting to note that the trachea and main stem bronchi appears to be spared.
evidence: Observed through morphological analysis.

claim: Most cysts in Yap mutants also expressed SOX9.
source: Moreover, most cysts also expressed SOX9.
evidence: Observed through immunostaining.

claim: Cyst formation due to loss of mechanical force may be prone to occur at the distal tips of the lung.
source: It is also possible that a fundamental difference in the mechanical properties of lung epithelial cells exists in different regions of the lung. In this scenario, cyst formation due to loss of mechanical force may be prone to occur at the distal tips of the lung.
evidence: Speculated based on the observation that cysts primarily form in distal regions.

claim: Lung epithelial cells in the proximal part of the airway may receive mechanical restraints from neighboring cells and cyst formation is less frequent.
source: By contrast, lung epithelial cells in the proximal part of the airway may receive mechanical restraints from neighboring cells and cyst formation is less frequent.
evidence: Speculated based on the observation that proximal regions are less affected.

claim: Loss of Fzd2 resulted in reduced apical pMLC expression.
source: Interestingly, a previous study reported distal cyst formation in Frizzled 2 (Fzd2)-deficient lungs (Kadzik et al., 2014). Loss of Fzd2 also resulted in reduced apical pMLC expression (Kadzik et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: Non-canonical Wnt signaling through its receptor Fzd2 regulates epithelial cell behavior necessary for lung branching.
source: These findings led to a model in which non-canonical Wnt signaling through its receptor Fzd2 regulates epithelial cell behavior necessary for lung branching.
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: Wnt signaling could impinge upon YAP during branching morphogenesis.
source: This raises the interesting possibility that Wnt signaling could impinge upon YAP during branching morphogenesis.
evidence: Speculated based on similarities between Fzd2 and Yap mutant phenotypes.

claim: Nuclear YAP in SOX2+ cells at the 'transition zone' was proposed to directly induce Sox2 expression in a previous study.
source: Moreover, nuclear YAP in SOX2+ cells at the 'transition zone' was proposed in the published literature (Mahoney et al., 2014) to directly induce Sox2 expression.
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: The model of localized YAP activity in the transition zone is at odds with studies in other tissues where Hippo signaling exerts a general effect on all cells.
source: While attractive, this model seems to be at odds with studies in other tissues where Hippo signaling exerts a general effect on all cells.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with Hippo signaling in other tissues.

claim: The findings in this study contradict the predictions of localized YAP activity in the transition zone.
source: These findings contradict the predictions of localized YAP activity in the transition zone and instead support our model of a general effect of YAP on epithelial cell properties.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations showing widespread YAP activity and localized cyst formation with different Cre lines.

claim: The expression levels of Shh were reduced in Yap-deficient lungs.
source: The expression levels of Shh were reduced while Fgf10 was upregulated in Yap-deficient lungs.
evidence: Demonstrated by qPCR analysis.

claim: Fgf10 was upregulated in Yap-deficient lungs.
source: The expression levels of Shh were reduced while Fgf10 was upregulated in Yap-deficient lungs.
evidence: Demonstrated by qPCR analysis.

claim: The changes in Shh and Fgf10 expression are consistent with a negative regulatory relationship between Shh and Fgf10.
source: This is consistent with a negative regulatory relationship between Shh and Fgf10 (Pepicelli et al., 1998), which mediate important interactions between lung epithelium and mesenchyme.
evidence: Inferred from expression changes and cited literature.

claim: Shh and Fgf10 mediate important interactions between lung epithelium and mesenchyme.
source: This is consistent with a negative regulatory relationship between Shh and Fgf10 (Pepicelli et al., 1998), which mediate important interactions between lung epithelium and mesenchyme.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The use of ShhCre has contributed to the reduction in Shh expression levels.
source: Note that the use of ShhCre has contributed to the reduction in Shh expression levels although it is unlikely to be solely responsible for the low levels of Shh in the absence of Yap.
evidence: Inferred from the mechanism of Cre-mediated gene disruption.

claim: Control of actin and pMLC is mediated by the RhoA–ROCK cascade.
source: Control of actin and pMLC is mediated by the RhoA–ROCK cascade (Amano et al., 2010) (Figure 7S).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: The small GTPase Rho binds and activates ROCK.
source: The small GTPase Rho binds and activates ROCK (Rho-associated protein kinase).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of RhoA-ROCK signaling.

claim: ROCK is the major regulator of the actomyosin cytoskeleton.
source: ROCK is the major regulator of the actomyosin cytoskeleton and ROCK enhances myosin phosphorylation and consequently cellular contractility.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of ROCK function.

claim: ROCK enhances myosin phosphorylation and consequently cellular contractility.
source: ROCK is the major regulator of the actomyosin cytoskeleton and ROCK enhances myosin phosphorylation and consequently cellular contractility.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of ROCK function.

claim: RhoA activity is regulated by RhoGEF, which activates RhoA, and RhoGAP, which inhibits RhoA.
source: RhoA activity is regulated by RhoGEF (Rho guanine exchange factor), which activates RhoA, and RhoGAP (Rho GTP activating factor), which inhibits RhoA.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of RhoA regulation.

claim: Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ embryos were visibly smaller than their wild-type littermates.
source: Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ embryos were visibly smaller than their wild-type littermates and all of them had a short curly tail, which could be used to identify Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ embryos by their outer appearance.
evidence: Observed through phenotypic analysis.

claim: All Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ embryos had a short curly tail.
source: Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ embryos were visibly smaller than their wild-type littermates and all of them had a short curly tail, which could be used to identify Yapf/f; ShhCre/+ embryos by their outer appearance.
evidence: Observed through phenotypic analysis.

claim: Yapf/f; ShhCre/Cre mice (carrying two copies of ShhCre) exhibited the classical Hedgehog defects due to disruption of the Shh locus and died at various time points during embryonic development.
source: Of note, Yapf/f; ShhCre/Cre mice (carrying two copies of ShhCre) exhibited the classical Hedgehog defects due to disruption of the Shh locus and died at various time points during embryonic development (Chiang et al., 1996).
evidence: Observed through phenotypic analysis and cited from literature on Shh mutants.
